request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
HOSPITAL COURSE SUMMARY

Patient Name: [REDACTED]
Date of Admission: [REDACTED]
Date of Discharge: [REDACTED]
Length of Stay: [REDACTED]

CHIEF COMPLAINT: RUQ pain

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS:
The patient, a 26-year-old male, presented to the emergency department with a three-day history of RUQ pain, which worsened with food. Physical exam demonstrated focal RUQ peritonitis with a positive Murphy’s sign, but no rebound or guarding. Ultrasound revealed a stone in the gallbladder neck and no pericholecystic fluid. Surgery was consulted and the patient was offered outpatient follow-up for biliary colic.

PAST MEDICAL HISTORY:
The patient has a prior history of good health. No past medical conditions or significant illnesses were noted in the chart.

HOSPITAL COURSE:
The patient was monitored in the hospital for a brief period and discharged with a plan for outpatient follow-up for biliary colic. The following day, the patient returned to the emergency department with persistent pain and underwent cholecystectomy for cholecystitis.
DISCHARGE DIAGNOSIS: [diagnosis section withheld]
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS:
The patient is advised to take adequate rest and avoid heavy lifting for a few days. The surgical incisions should be kept clean and dry. The patient should follow the medication regimen as prescribed. The patient is instructed to return to the hospital if there are any signs of fever, redness, swelling, or discharge at the surgical site, or if the pain persists.

FOLLOW-UP:
The patient will have a follow-up appointment with the surgeon in approximately one week to assess postoperative recovery and discuss any further management or treatment options.

DISCHARGE CONDITION:
The patient was discharged in stable condition with the appropriate medical care and follow-up plan in place.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
The episode that ended in cholecystectomy was for cholecystitis with a gallbladder stone, so the principal diagnosis falls under calculus of the gallbladder with cholecystitis (K80). The first presentation was managed as biliary colic and the patient was discharged. The return visit, where the patient had persistent pain and underwent surgery, is the episode that established the diagnosis.

The ultrasound showed a stone in the gallbladder neck. The exam showed a positive Murphy's sign, and the final surgical diagnosis was cholecystitis. In ICD-10-AM, calculous cholecystitis is coded to K80.0 (acute cholecystitis with calculus) or K80.1 (other cholecystitis with calculus). Both sit in the three-character category K80.

CODE: K80
